The experiments covered a Reynolds number range from 10,000 to 172,000 and freestream turbulence intensities from 0.08% to 4%.

The intermittency transport model was able to reproduce the streamwise intermittency distribution of Dhawan and Narasimha and also produce a realistic variation of intermittency in the cross-stream direction.

The onset of attached flow transition was determined using a correlation in terms of turbulence intensity and acceleration parameter, while the onset of separated flow transition was predicted using a correlation in terms of turbulence intensity and momentum thickness Reynolds number at separation.
For the high freestream turbulence intensity (4%) cases, the computations predicted the onset of separation and reattachment slightly upstream of the experimental values.
For the low freestream turbulence intensity (1%) cases, the computations underpredicted the extent of the separation bubble compared to the experiments.
The computed total pressure loss coefficients were 2-3% higher than the experimental data for the Re=25,000 and 50,000 cases.
As the Reynolds number increased from 50,000 to 100,000, the size of the separation bubble decreased, and the onset of transition moved upstream on the suction surface of the blade.
The model was able to capture the laminar, separated, and reattached regions of the flow in the computed velocity profiles along the suction surface of the Pack B blade.
The Pack B blade is an ideal test case for validating transition and turbulence models for low-pressure turbine applications due to its sensitivity to changes in flow conditions.
Laminar separation on low-pressure turbine blades can cause unpredicted losses and substantial drops in efficiency, which is important to address for the design of more efficient jet engines.

The intermittency transport model was previously validated against ERCOFTAC benchmark experiments, low-pressure turbine experiments, and separated and transitional boundary layer experiments with success.
The multiblock grid system used in the computations had first y+ less than 0.5 near solid walls to ensure accurate capture of the flow details.

Menter's SST turbulence model was used as the baseline model to compute the eddy viscosity and other turbulent quantities, as it produces almost fully turbulent flow in the leading edge of the boundary layer.
The intermittency is incorporated into the computations by multiplying the eddy viscosity obtained from the turbulence model with the intermittency factor.
The onset of transition locations and the reattachment locations were not reported in the experiments, so they were extracted from the experimental pressure coefficient data.
